cues.text: Section two: Performance measurement.
IT performance is the degree to which technology delivers reliable, efficient and useful outcomes.
Consider a fast application that loses customer transactions.
However quick it is, it is not performing well.
Performance, in this broader sense, includes speed, capacity, reliability, availability, security, quality and user satisfaction.
Now let us separate a few terms.
A metric is simply a measurement.
A key performance indicator, or KPI, is a measurement selected because it indicates progress toward an important objective.
For example, CPU utilisation is a metric, while successful payment percentage may be a KPI for a payment business.
Two further ideas go with these.
A target states the desired result, and a baseline describes the starting point.
The source gives a table of common KPIs.
I will go through it row by row, with the meaning and the example for each.
Response time is the time taken to complete a request.
An example is 250 milliseconds.
Throughput is the work completed per unit of time.
An example is 500 transactions per second.
Availability is the proportion of agreed time during which the service is available.
An example is 99.95 percent.
MTTD is the mean time to detect incidents.
An example is 5 minutes.
MTTR is the mean time to restore or resolve incidents.
An example is 30 minutes.
MTBF is the mean operating time between failures.
An example is 200 hours.
FCR is first contact resolution.
An example is 80 percent.
CSAT is customer satisfaction.
An example is 90 percent positive.
And SLA attainment is the proportion of cases meeting agreed targets.
An example is 97 percent.
When you use any of these, define the measurement window, the eligible population and the calculation rules.
Note that MTTR can mean repair, recovery or resolution depending on context, so use consistent definitions.
FCR measures eligible issues resolved at first contact, without escalation or repeat contact, under the chosen rules.
Next, worked calculations.
Suppose a service runs for a 30-day month, which is 720 hours, and experiences 90 minutes of downtime.
That is 1.5 hours.
Availability equals 720 minus 1.5, divided by 720, multiplied by 100, which gives 99.7917 percent.
Now a second table, showing the downtime allowed in 30 days for each availability target.
At 99 percent, the allowance is 7.2 hours.
At 99.9 percent, it is 43.2 minutes.
At 99.99 percent, it is 4.32 minutes.
And at 99.999 percent, it is 25.92 seconds.
These figures assume continuous service and no excluded downtime.
Also, availability does not imply zero failures.
A system can fail frequently but recover quickly, or fail rarely and take a long time to recover.
Now some more examples.
If three incidents take 4, 8 and 12 minutes to detect, then MTTD equals 24 divided by 3, which is 8 minutes.
If their recovery times are 20, 30 and 40 minutes, then MTTR is 30 minutes.
And if 80 of 100 eligible support incidents are resolved at first contact, then FCR is 80 percent.
For a repairable system with stable failure and repair characteristics, approximate availability equals MTBF divided by the sum of MTBF and MTTR.
If MTBF is 200 hours and MTTR is 2 hours, availability is about 99.01 percent.
Finally, a caution about averages.
Latency averages can hide poor experiences.
A p95 latency of 800 milliseconds means that approximately 95 percent of measured requests finish within 800 milliseconds.
So monitor tail latency, error rates and throughput together.
A system that rejects most requests may appear fast if only successful requests are measured.
